title: Initiative Return on Investment Ranking
real_world_story:
A corporate financial planning software ranks N proposed departmental initiatives. Each initiative has an integer project_id, an integer cost, and an integer expected_return. The Return on Investment (ROI) ratio is defined as expected_return / cost. To present a prioritized investment roadmap to executive leadership, the software must rank projects:
1. Primarily in descending order of ROI ratio.
2. Secondarily in ascending order of cost (lower cost preferred when ROI is tied).
3. Tertiarily in ascending order of project_id as a final tie-breaker.
problem_statement: Given N initiatives, each with project_id, cost, and expected_return, sort the initiatives according to the specified multi-criteria rules. Print the sorted project IDs separated by a single space.
task: Sort the initiatives by ROI ratio descending, cost ascending, and project_id ascending, then print the ordered IDs separated by a space.
input_format:
The first line contains a single integer N, the number of initiatives.
The next N lines each contain three space-separated integers: project_id, cost, and expected_return.
output_format: Print the sorted sequence of project IDs on a single line, separated by a single space.

examples.explanation: ROI ratios: 101: 25/10 = 2.5; 102: 60/20 = 3.0; 103: 15/5 = 3.0; 104: 20/8 = 2.5. Projects 102 and 103 tie at ROI 3.0; 103 has lower cost (5 < 20), so 103 precedes 102. Projects 101 and 104 tie at ROI 2.5; 104 has lower cost (8 < 10), so 104 precedes 101. Final order: 103 102 104 101.
Both initiatives have identical ROI (3.0) and cost (10); tie-breaking by project_id places 10 before 20.

real_world_takeaway: Using integer cross-multiplication (r1 * c2 vs r2 * c1) when sorting financial ratios eliminates floating-point rounding errors in investment ranking engines.
